takeaway: In the 4.4 million main-corpus methods most measurements are tiny (64% have CC 1, 63% have CogC 0, 67% have MaxNest 0) with very long tails; the plot is descriptive and no distribution is fitted.

CC and CogC rank corpus methods almost identically (Spearman 0.99) and MaxNest is close to both (0.94), while LOC is related at about 0.72; the 34 constructed survey snippets show weaker relationships, especially between CC and MaxNest.

Without the methods at each metric's lowest value the corpus correlations fall but stay positive: CC and CogC 0.92, MaxNest 0.64 to 0.76 with the other control-flow metrics, LOC 0.73 to 0.74 with CC and CogC and 0.53 with MaxNest; in the 29 to 32 survey snippets that remain they range from 0.36 (CC with MaxNest) to 0.90 (CogC with MaxNest).
In the 44 survey pairs the metrics almost never order a pair in opposite directions (0-7% of pairs, never for CC and CogC); most differences are one metric tying while the other separates.

For random pairs of corpus methods the metrics order a pair in opposite directions in under 6% of pairs; the main difference is ties, since most random pairs are trivial and CC, CogC and MaxNest often tie.

Among non-trivial methods (CC >= 3) CC and CogC mostly agree on direction (70% concordant, 8% discordant), while LOC is discordant with CC, CogC and MaxNest in 15% to 18% of pairs and MaxNest ties on many pairs the others separate.
CC ties on 41% of the survey pairs and MaxNest on 36%, against 18% for CogC and LOC.
Two random corpus methods tie on CC 44% of the time, on CogC 43%, on MaxNest 50% and on LOC only 12%, because most methods are tiny.

Once methods at a metric's lowest value (CC 1, CogC 0, LOC 1, MaxNest 0) are removed, two random corpus methods tie on CC 20% of the time, CogC 18%, LOC 13% and MaxNest 48%, so most of the CC and CogC ties in fig04b come from trivial methods but MaxNest still ties often.

One shared component explains 89% of the variation between the four metrics in the corpus and 80% in the 34 constructed survey snippets; this is supporting evidence and does not show the metrics are equivalent.
CogC agrees with participants most often (57% of 750 responses) and CC least (43%); every metric is above the agreement expected by chance (black diamond), CC by the smallest margin.

Across every measurement recorded for the survey snippets, Halstead effort (58%) and CogC (57%) agree with participants most often, with overlapping intervals; CC (43%) is the lowest of the size and structure measurements, and fan-out, identifier words, comments, Javadoc, recursion and parameter count are close to the agreement expected by chance.

When a participant chose a side, CC tied on 37% of those responses and MaxNest on 34%, against 15% for CogC and 14% for LOC; the share of responses where a metric pointed the other way was similar for all four (16-27%).

When a metric does separate the two methods and the participant chooses a side, all four metrics are right about 70% of the time (68-75%), so CC's lower overall agreement comes from tying, not from pointing the wrong way.

Where CC ties but CogC separates the pair (10 pairs), 83% of decisive responses (123 of 149) chose the method CogC rates lower, and 9 of the 10 pairs are above 50%; the same holds for MaxNest (83%, 6 of 7 pairs) and LOC (66%, 8 of 11 pairs).

Where CC ties and LOC separates (11 pairs) participants took LOC's side in 66% of decisive responses; in the two pairs where they point in opposite directions the split (57% CC, 43% LOC) is not significant.

No pair has CC and MaxNest pointing in opposite directions; where CC ties and MaxNest separates (7 pairs) participants took MaxNest's side in 82% of decisive responses, but where MaxNest ties and CC separates (5 pairs) only 52% took CC's side.
CogC and LOC point in opposite directions on three pairs, where participants sided with CogC in 66% of decisive responses (not significant after correction for multiple tests).
CogC and MaxNest point in opposite directions on a single pair, where participants sided with CogC in 88% of decisive responses; this rests on one pair.
No pair has LOC and MaxNest pointing in opposite directions; where MaxNest ties and LOC separates (8 pairs) participants took LOC's side in 46% of decisive responses.

Every metric agrees much more often when the lower measurement is on the left (A) than on the right (B), and only about 10% of the time when it ties, because a tie can agree only with 'No difference'.

CC ties about as often when participants saw a big difference (37%) as when they saw none (35%), whereas CogC, LOC and MaxNest tie less often on the pairs participants rated 'much' different (11%, 9% and 27%) than on those rated 'slightly' different (17%, 18% and 39%).

Dropping any one of the 10 tasks keeps CogC the highest-agreeing metric (54% to 59% across the drops) and keeps the order CogC > LOC > MaxNest > CC in 9 of 10; the CogC-minus-LOC gap falls to 0.3 points when task 3 is dropped.

CC and MaxNest separate 63% and 66% of the pairs participants took a side on, against 86% for CogC and LOC, while direction accuracy is similar for all four (CC 69%, CogC 72%, LOC 68%, MaxNest 75%, intervals overlapping): the agreement gap comes from separating the pair, not from direction.

Across the 13 measures, agreement falls as the tie rate rises (Halstead effort and CogC tie on about 11% and 15% and agree on 58% and 57%; CC ties on 36% and agrees on 43%; parameter count ties on 100% and agrees on 10%).

With all four metrics in one cumulative-link mixed model only MaxNest's coefficient excludes zero (3.1, 95% CI 1.4 to 4.9); CogC is borderline (2.1, -0.1 to 4.2) and CC and LOC are indistinguishable from zero, but the predictors are correlated up to 0.84 so each coefficient is imprecise.

On the first two principal components (96% of the variance), 11 of the 34 survey snippets lie outside the ellipse holding 90% of corpus methods, and all four metric arrows point the same way along PC1.
On the seven pairs where all four metrics tie, 81% of decisive responses (61 of 75) chose the later version as less complex; six of the seven pairs are above 50% and one (Q5C, naming) is at 50%.

In the within-task Bradley-Terry model most variants are judged less complex than their original, 03-V2 is judged more complex (+0.9, interval above zero) and 05-V3 is indistinguishable from its original (+0.1); within tasks the latent scores track MaxNest (rho 0.87), CogC (0.82), LOC (0.73) and CC (0.60) in that order.
Counting each pair once, every metric's measurement difference correlates positively with the perceived difference (Spearman 0.51 for CC to 0.70 for MaxNest).

Dropping participants who missed screening questions changes agreement by under one point; dropping tied or No-difference responses raises every metric's agreement and changes the ranking (MaxNest is highest among pairs it separates), so overall agreement and direction accuracy tell different stories.
Agreement rises with self-reported experience for all four metrics, but not significantly after correction (Holm p = .38), and the 'none' (5) and 'large' (3) groups are very small.
14 of 24 refactored variants were judged less complex more often than not, against 1 of 10 originals (03-ORIG); clear exceptions are 03-ORIG, which won, and 03-V2, a refactor that lost.
Versions with the highest CC in their task were judged less complex in 40% of comparisons on average, against 66% for those with the lowest CC (Spearman -0.54 across the 34 versions, descriptive).

Versions with the highest CogC in their task were judged less complex in 34% of comparisons on average, against 70% for those with the lowest CogC (Spearman -0.74 across the 34 versions, descriptive).
Versions with the highest LOC in their task were judged less complex in 37% of comparisons on average, against 67% for those with the lowest LOC (Spearman -0.60 across the 34 versions, descriptive).

Versions with the highest MaxNest in their task were judged less complex in 34% of comparisons on average, against 68% for those with the lowest MaxNest (Spearman -0.75 across the 34 versions, descriptive).

After correction for multiple tests four refactors were significantly preferred to their original and one (03-V2) was significantly rejected; the rest are inconclusive, mostly because many pairs have few responses.

Refactors were preferred in roughly two thirds of decisive responses whether or not a metric's measurement fell (for example CC 65% when it fell and 71% when unchanged), so a falling measurement did not clearly mean a stronger preference.

Removing branching or nesting, and adding comments, were the changes preferred most; extraction and naming changed perceptions little, and shortening code while keeping CC and CogC (volume) or replacing recursion with a loop made code feel more complex. Descriptive: each kind of change rests on one to four variants.

Overall 54% of decisive responses chose the right-hand method, but in the 20 pairs without an original 65% chose the left, so the lean follows which version is shown (refactors were usually on the right) rather than the side of the screen.

Broader set of corpus metrics: control-flow metrics (CC, CogC, nesting) form one very tight group and size metrics (LOC, words, Halstead) another; the two groups are related to each other at about 0.7, while naming and comment measures are only weakly related to either.
With the broader metric sets the first component explains about half of the variation in the corpus sample (52%), so the broader set carries more than one dimension.
Corpus methods and survey snippets plotted on the first two components (the survey snippets span the range of the typical corpus method but are not a random sample).

Response-level version of the tie share: because pairs differ in how many people saw them, it differs from the pair-level share.
